recipe.history:
Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla) is one of the oldest cultivated leafy vegetables in the world, with roots stretching back to ancient Sicily and the broader Mediterranean basin. Despite its common name, chard is not Swiss in origin — the name is attributed to a 19th-century Swiss botanist who formally classified the plant in botanical literature, cementing a geographic misnomer that has persisted ever since. Ancient Greeks and Romans prized it as both food and medicine, crediting it with restorative and purifying properties. It grew prolifically along the coastal soils of North Africa and Southern Europe, where the combination of heat, salt air, and well-drained earth produced leaves of extraordinary depth and color. By the medieval period, chard had spread across the Islamic world and into the kitchens of Moorish Spain, where it was braised with garlic, vinegar, and pine nuts — a preparation that still echoes in modern Catalan cooking.

Swiss chard arrived in the Americas through the hands of European settlers and, later, through waves of immigration from Italy, Portugal, and Greece in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It found particular purchase in the home gardens of immigrant communities in California, the Northeast, and the Gulf Coast, where the climate permitted near-year-round cultivation. American chefs largely ignored it in favor of more fashionable greens until the farm-to-table movement of the 1980s and 1990s brought it back into professional kitchens with renewed urgency. Burger culture caught on more slowly, but inventive cooks eventually recognized that chard — especially when charred hard in a screaming-hot cast-iron pan with olive oil, salt, and a touch of red pepper — offered something no lettuce could: a bitter, smoky, slightly caramelized counterpoint that cuts through the richness of beef fat with surgical precision. It transforms the burger from a simple sandwich into a study in contrast.

I first had a version of this burger at a tiny counter restaurant on a gray Tuesday in October, the kind of afternoon where the city feels like it is folding in on itself and you need something warm and slightly reckless to remind you that you are still alive. The cook slapped the chard down on the flat-top with an almost contemptuous confidence, and it hissed and blackened at the edges within seconds. She placed it on top of the patty without ceremony, tucked it under a brioche crown, and slid the plate across the counter without looking up. I ate it standing at the window, watching the rain, and I remember thinking that this was exactly what a burger was supposed to feel like — not pretty, not precious, just deeply, uncomplicatedly right. I have been chasing that specific feeling ever since, which is probably why I make this one more than any other.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a matter of preference — it is a matter of physics and respect. At medium rare, the muscle fibers have relaxed just enough to release their juices without fully expelling them; the fat has rendered into the meat without burning away; the Maillard crust on the exterior is fully developed while the interior remains blush-pink, tender, and faintly mineral. Cooking a burger beyond this point is a slow erasure — each degree above 135°F pushes more moisture out, tightens the proteins further, and moves the patty incrementally closer to the texture of a hockey puck. A well-sourced, properly seasoned patty cooked to medium rare needs nothing to hide behind. It carries its own argument. The charred chard understands this, which is why they belong together.
ingredients: 300g (2 1/2 cups) bread flour, plus more for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
85g (6 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
450g (1 lb) ground beef chuck, 80/20 fat ratio
1 tsp flaky sea salt (for seasoning just before cooking)
1 large bunch Swiss chard (rainbow or standard green), stems trimmed
Flaky sea salt and black pepper to taste
200ml (3/4 cup + 1 tbsp) neutral oil (such as grapeseed or light olive oil)
FOR THE CRISPY CHARD CHIPS (optional garnish):
4–6 small inner chard leaves, patted completely dry
4 slices aged white cheddar or Gruyère
Neutral oil or clarified butter for cooking the patty
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — ACTIVATE YEAST: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Stir gently and let sit for 8–10 minutes until foamy and fragrant. If it does not foam, your yeast is dead — start over with fresh yeast.

2. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — MIX THE DOUGH: Add 2 eggs and the flour and salt to the yeast mixture. Using the dough hook attachment, mix on low speed for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms. Increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes until the dough comes together into a smooth mass.

3. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — ADD BUTTER: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is fully incorporated before adding the next. This process takes 8–10 minutes. The dough will look broken and greasy at first — keep going. Once all butter is incorporated, increase speed to medium-high and knead for 5 more minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls cleanly from the sides of the bowl.

4. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — FIRST RISE: Shape the dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or overnight. Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the dough easier to handle.

5. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — SHAPE AND SECOND RISE: Remove dough from refrigerator. Divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 170g each). Working quickly while the dough is still cold, shape each piece into a tight ball by pulling the sides under and pinching the bottom. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let rise at room temperature for 2–2.5 hours until puffy and nearly doubled.

6. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — BAKE: Preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make an egg wash. Brush the tops of the buns gently and evenly. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16–19 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through, until deeply golden brown. Cool on a wire rack for at least 20 minutes before slicing.

7. MAKE THE GARLIC AIOLI: Place garlic cloves on a cutting board, sprinkle with salt, and use the flat side of a knife to smash and mince them into a smooth paste, working the salt into the garlic repeatedly. Transfer to a medium bowl. Add egg yolks, Dijon mustard, and lemon juice and whisk vigorously to combine. Very slowly — drop by drop at first — whisk in the neutral oil. Once the emulsion is established (after about 1/4 of the oil has been incorporated), you can add the remaining oil in a thin, steady stream, whisking constantly. Finish by whisking in the extra-virgin olive oil. Taste and adjust salt and lemon. Refrigerate until ready to use.

8. MAKE THE CHARD CHIPS (if using): Preheat oven to 325°F / 163°C. Toss small, dry chard leaves with olive oil and a pinch of salt. Spread in a single layer on a parchment-lined baking sheet, making sure leaves do not overlap. Bake for 12–15 minutes until crisp and deeply colored but not black. Watch carefully — they go from perfect to burnt quickly. Set aside.

9. PREPARE THE BEEF PATTY BLEND: Combine the ground chuck and ground short rib in a bowl. Using your hands, mix just until the two meats are evenly distributed — do not overwork. Divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 155g each). Press each portion gently into a patty about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty — this prevents the patty from doming during cooking. Place on a plate lined with parchment and refrigerate, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes. Do NOT season yet.

10. PREPARE THE CHARD FOR CHARRING: Wash the chard and dry it thoroughly — excess moisture will cause steaming rather than charring. Separate the leaves from the stems. Cut the leaves into large, roughly hand-sized pieces. Thinly slice the stems and set aside separately.

11. CHAR THE CHARD: Heat a large cast-iron skillet over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly — at least 3 minutes of preheating. Add olive oil. It should shimmer and begin smoking almost immediately. Working in batches to avoid crowding, add the chard leaves to the pan in a single layer. Do not touch them for 60–90 seconds, allowing them to blacken at the edges and char against the surface. Toss once, cook for another 30 seconds, then push to the side of the pan. Add the sliced stems, garlic, and red pepper flakes. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until garlic is golden and stems have softened. Recombine everything in the pan, deglaze with sherry vinegar (it will spit — stand back), toss once more, and transfer to a bowl. Season with flaky salt and black pepper. Keep warm.

12. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Wipe the cast-iron skillet with a paper towel and return it to high heat until smoking. Season both sides of the cold patties generously with flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking — not before. Add a thin film of neutral oil or clarified butter to the pan. Place patties in the pan dimple-side up and do not move them for 2 minutes. Flip once. Place a slice of cheese on each patty. Cook for 1.5–2 minutes more. Check the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — you are targeting 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. The patty should have a deep mahogany crust and a yielding, soft feel when pressed. Remove from heat and rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes — the carryover will bring the temperature up slightly, but it will stay in the medium-rare window. Do not cook beyond 135°F under any circumstances.

13. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice the brioche buns in half. Place cut-side down in the still-hot skillet (no extra fat needed) and toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Remove immediately.

14. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous layer of garlic aioli on both the cut top and bottom of each toasted bun. Place the patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Pile a generous mound of charred chard directly on top of the patty, allowing it to spill over the edges. If using, lay 2–3 chard chips on top of the chard for additional crunch and a visual contrast of textures. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt over the whole assembly. Place the top bun on firmly, press down lightly, and serve immediately.
